draft.title: Diffusion, gas pressure and expansion
card: Diffusion
Particles are always moving, so they spread out from where there are many of them to where there are fewer. This happens in gases and liquids, and you can smell a perfume across a room because of it.
Gas pressure
Gas particles move fast and hit the walls of their container. Billions of tiny hits push on the walls, and this push is gas pressure.
Heating
Heating gives particles more energy, so they move faster. A gas in a closed container then hits the walls harder and more often, so its pressure rises.
Expansion
When most substances are heated, their particles move further apart. The particles themselves do not get bigger, but the substance takes up more space. This is expansion.
draft.remember: Moving particles spread out, hit walls to make pressure, and move further apart when heated.

a.q: Why does the smell of baking bread spread through a house?
opts: Moving particles spread from many to fewer
Smell particles are pushed out by gas pressure
The air particles all expand when they warm up
Smell particles are heavier so they sink and spread
a.why: Bread particles are always moving, so they spread out into the rest of the house by diffusion. Gas pressure is about particles hitting walls, not about spreading smells through a room.
a.clue: Think about where there are many particles and where there are few.

b.q: Tom leaves a sealed, rigid bottle of air in a hot car. The air inside heats up. Why does the pressure inside the bottle rise?
opts: The particles move faster and hit the walls harder
The particles get bigger and push on the walls
The particles slow down and crowd onto the walls
The bottle gets bigger and the particles diffuse out
b.why: Heating gives the particles more energy, so they move faster and hit the walls harder and more often. The particles do not get bigger. Expansion means they move further apart, not that each one grows.
b.clue: What does heating do to the energy of the particles?

a.best: Moving particles spread from many to fewer

b.best: The particles move faster and hit the walls harder

problems.detail: The clue ('where there are many particles and where there are few') echoes the right option's own words 'from many to fewer', so a student can match it without understanding diffusion.
The why says 'Bread particles' spread through the house. It is smell particles given off by the bread that diffuse, not particles of the bread itself, so this could mislead.
